articles.author: NixCon
articles.summary: finix – making space for multiple nix operating systems aanderse After another year of building and daily-driving [finix](https://github.com/finix-community/finix), I remain interested in what it means for `nix` to support multiple operating system designs and philosophies. In this talk, I will shar
articles.content:
finix – making space for multiple nix operating systems

aanderse

After another year of building and daily-driving [finix](https://github.com/finix-community/finix), I remain interested in what it means for `nix` to support multiple operating system designs and philosophies. In this talk, I will share some lessons from my experiences with `finix`, and beyond, and make the case that healthy ecosystems benefit from diversity.

`nixos` remains an extraordinary achievement. But if the ideas behind `nix` are truly powerful, they should be able to adapt to different technical philosophies and communities, rather than requiring everyone to converge on a single vision. By creating space for alternative approaches, we can bring those ideas to people who might otherwise never adopt them at all.

Talk page: https://talks.nixcon.org/nixcon-2026/talk/GQFKXA/

articles.content:
server apps commodified: digital autonomy for the masses

Kiara Grouwstra

While nixpkgs has made lots of software reproducible, most users of devices experience technical barriers in switching to open-source software still.

In this talk, Fediversity developer @kiara explains the shortcomings of the GDPR's right to data portability, and how we can do better while bringing Nix to the masses.

It will further touch on:

- how Nix services can facilitate micro-service architectures
- how we can use GUIs to configure Nix modules
- using Nix to make portable infrastructure

articles.title: NixCon 2026 - Trampolining Nix, or how I nearly lost my mind fighting the Nix evaluator
articles.author: NixCon
articles.summary: Trampolining Nix, or how I nearly lost my mind fighting the Nix evaluator Mika Bohinen I wanted to see how far I could take Nix as a programming language, so nix-effects grew to include a small language with effect handlers, a type checker and an evaluator, all written in Nix. This talk is about the
articles.content:
Trampolining Nix, or how I nearly lost my mind fighting the Nix evaluator

Mika Bohinen

I wanted to see how far I could take Nix as a programming language, so nix-effects grew to include a small language with effect handlers, a type checker and an evaluator, all written in Nix. This talk is about the unreasonable amount of work that went into getting it to run the next step.

We start with a small effectful program and the recursive driver that runs it. Nix keeps the waiting calls even when they have nothing left to do, so we look for a builtin to handle repetition. A strict fold works when we already have a list to traverse, but a general interpreter that needs to decide what happens next based on previous state needs something more, so we borrow `builtins.genericClosure`.

Then we ask for the result, which turns out to be a separate endeavor. We follow the deferred additions, make evaluation happen before advancing, and discover what forcing too much costs. Deeply nested types bring another problem, because forcing a function doesn’t run its body. Making that work explicit gives us control over execution, but the borrowed driver is still keeping every state we ever visited.

We’ll work through small runnable examples to see how far genericClosure gets us, what it takes to make the results usable, and why I ended up wanting a native loop in Nix. No type theory knowledge required, though some sympathy for someone who did all this to get a while loop would be appreciated.

Talk page: https://talks.nixcon.org/nixcon-2026/talk/3AGQJD/

Recorded at NixCon 2026.
Licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/

articles.title: NixCon 2026 - The thunk trap, why your Nix loop crashes after it finishes
articles.author: NixCon
articles.summary: The thunk trap, why your Nix loop crashes after it finishes Mika Bohinen `builtins.foldl'` is strict, which sounds reassuring until your fold finishes and reading the result causes a stack overflow. This talk takes one small problem from carrying interpreter state through Nix and reduces it to a cou
articles.content:
The thunk trap, why your Nix loop crashes after it finishes

Mika Bohinen

`builtins.foldl'` is strict, which sounds reassuring until your fold finishes and reading the result causes a stack overflow. This talk takes one small problem from carrying interpreter state through Nix and reduces it to a counter in an attribute set.

We’ll see why the fold evaluates each record while leaving its additions suspended, then fix it by computing the total before returning the next record. We’ll also compare `seq` and `deepSeq`, including what happens when forcing everything reaches a field we never needed. It is rather a lot of trouble to go through to add one.

Talk page: https://talks.nixcon.org/nixcon-2026/talk/VSKERY/

articles.title: NixCon 2026 - Why I changed my mind about flakes
articles.author: NixCon
articles.summary: Why I changed my mind about flakes Valentin Gagarin (@fricklerhandwerk) Technically speaking, flakes address problems with distributing Nix-based software projects: hermetic evaluation, managing dependencies on remote sources, and a standard interface for consumers, all shipped as batteries included
articles.content:
Why I changed my mind about flakes

Valentin Gagarin (@fricklerhandwerk)

Technically speaking, flakes address problems with distributing Nix-based software projects: hermetic evaluation, managing dependencies on remote sources, and a standard interface for consumers, all shipped as batteries included.

Sounds simple enough. Yet, the introduction of flakes became a source of internet drama – and 7 years later, flakes are still experimental. This talk traces how we got into a controversy that was never quite resolved, and makes the case that it was never really about flakes.

My goal is to highlight what I suspect is an underlying failure of communication, and to serve a healthy dose of unsolicited opinion on how we can do better in the future.

Talk page: https://talks.nixcon.org/nixcon-2026/talk/WEADU3/

Recorded at NixCon 2026.

articles.title: NixCon 2026 - netbox-nixos: automatically turning NetBox devices into NixOS configurations
articles.author: NixCon
articles.summary: netbox-nixos: automatically turning NetBox devices into NixOS configurations Kierán Meinhardt, Jacek Galowicz **Slides:** https://github.com/applicative-systems/netbox-nixos/blob/10625b1352260d3a60113443034f8a4ebce34fe2/docs/netbox-nixos-krakow-nixcon.pdf NetBox has become a widely-used source of tr
articles.content:
netbox-nixos: automatically turning NetBox devices into NixOS configurations

Kierán Meinhardt, Jacek Galowicz

**Slides:** https://github.com/applicative-systems/netbox-nixos/blob/10625b1352260d3a60113443034f8a4ebce34fe2/docs/netbox-nixos-krakow-nixcon.pdf

NetBox has become a widely-used source of truth for datacentre and network infrastructure: devices, interfaces, IP addresses, prefixes, VLANs.
When those devices run NixOS, you'll want that data reflected in your NixOS configurations. Traditionally, the NixOS configuration lives in a repository and NetBox is treated as just another data source. If not managed very carefully, this results in error-prone maintenance and a steady supply of configuration drift.
netbox-nixos inverts that relationship and makes NetBox authoritative for NixOS configuration as well. Every NixOS device in NetBox is rendered into a NixOS configuration, served from a flake endpoint under NetBox's domain. Deploying a host is then just:

`$ nixos-rebuild switch --flake https://my.netbox/nixos#myDevice --target-host root@myDevice`

No repository round-trip, no drift. And as a bonus, non-Nix operators can manage host configuration directly through NetBox's UI.
In this talk we introduce netbox-nixos, show how a device configured in NetBox derives a complete NixOS configuration, and cover the questions this immediately raises: how NetBox's data model maps onto NixOS options, where the boundary sits between NetBox-owned network configuration and the modules you still write yourself, and what serving a flake from a live web service means for reproducibility and trust.

Talk page: https://talks.nixcon.org/nixcon-2026/talk/LQNN3Q/

Recorded at NixCon 2026.
Licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/

articles.author: NixCon
articles.summary: Declarative Frontiers: Running Kubernetes on RISC-V with NixOS Bruce Gain, Liang Yuning An open alternative to x86 and ARM shows promise: the RISC-V architecture is transitioning from an academic curiosity to a serious contender for edge and cloud workloads. However, deploying a complex cloud native
articles.content:
Declarative Frontiers: Running Kubernetes on RISC-V with NixOS

Bruce Gain, Liang Yuning

An open alternative to x86 and ARM shows promise: the RISC-V architecture is transitioning from an academic curiosity to a serious contender for edge and cloud workloads. However, deploying a complex cloud native stack like Kubernetes on RISC-V remains a minefield of fragmented kernel trees, slow native compilation on low-power Single Board Computers (SBCs), and missing upstream package suppor.
We demonstrates why NixOS can be idealfor bootstrapping emerging hardware architectures. We showcase how Nix’s native support for cross-compilation, flakes, and declarative kernel customization allows us to bypass the pain of native RISC-V builds entirely. We will share raw, unvarnished performance data comparing RISC-V Kubernetes nodes to their ARM counterparts, evaluating CPU/memory overhead and network limitations with Nix. Finally, we map out the "rough edges"—including Go runtime quirks and missing nixpkgs dependencies.

Talk page: https://talks.nixcon.org/nixcon-2026/talk/FCAMUG/

Recorded at NixCon 2026.

articles.summary: Nix for Cloud Native Platform Engineering: From Imperative Templating to Functional Derivation Arik Grahl **Slides**: [arik-grahl.de/talks/nixcon-2026](https://www.arik-grahl.de/talks/nixcon-2026) The Kubernetes ecosystem currently lacks a unified model for pure and reproducible deployments. Industr
articles.content:
Nix for Cloud Native Platform Engineering: From Imperative Templating to Functional Derivation

Arik Grahl

**Slides**: [arik-grahl.de/talks/nixcon-2026](https://www.arik-grahl.de/talks/nixcon-2026)

The Kubernetes ecosystem currently lacks a unified model for pure and reproducible deployments. Industry standards like Helm and Dockerfiles rely on impure templating and imperative definitions, creating non-deterministic side effects and opaque dependency trees. Often, the industry attempts to mitigate this by adding layers of orchestration (Internal Developer Platforms, GitOps controllers), which can inadvertently increase complexity without addressing the underlying fragility.

This talk demonstrates how to apply Nix’s functional purity to this landscape. By organizing a platform's entire catalogue as a Nix monorepository, inspired by the architecture of nixpkgs, we can shift from managing state to deriving it, achieving total reproducibility for the entire cloud-native stack.

We will explore how Kubenix leverages the OpenAPI specification to treat Kubernetes manifests and Helm charts as Nix expressions, replacing traditional YAML templating with a strongly-typed approach. To address the build layer, we examine how `dockerTools` brings Nix’s hermetic, network-isolated sandboxing to the OCI ecosystem. By treating containers as first-class dependencies, we can ensure fully reproducible artifacts, optimize storage via shared OCI layers, and generate accurate SBOMs and provenance attestations as natural byproducts. Finally, we will see how the NixOS module system serves as a flexible composition layer for the scalable orchestration of complex cluster configurations.

Let’s stop templating our cloud-native infrastructure and start deriving it with Nix: purely functional, hermetically sealed, and truly reproducible.

Talk page: https://talks.nixcon.org/nixcon-2026/talk/B7HA7F/

Recorded at NixCon 2026.
